query: For titanium alloys used as structural materials, formulate one hypothesis for an intervention that could increase surface hardness and wear resistance. Specify the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to the untreated alloy, the service or test conditions under which the effect should hold, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a controlled experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Sequential application of low‐temperature plasma nitriding followed by laser shock peening (LSP) will yield a densified, hard nitride surface with reduced roughness and enhanced compressive residual stresses, thereby significantly increasing both the surface hardness and wear resistance of Ti‑6Al‑4V alloy used in structural applications.
generation.material_initial_state: Ti‑6Al‑4V alloy in its as‐received annealed state (typically exhibiting a Widmanstätten microstructure).
generation.intervention: First, perform low‐temperature plasma nitriding (e.g., around 600 °C for 24 hours) to form a thin, uniform Ti‑N/Ti2N layer with minimal induced brittleness. Immediately afterward, apply laser shock peening using high pulse energy (e.g., ~7 J per pulse) to rework the surface morphology, reduce roughness, and impart beneficial compressive residual stresses.
generation.conditions: The expected improvements should hold during ambient-temperature cyclic wear tests (such as pin-on-disk under moderate loads) and fatigue testing that simulates structural service conditions at moderate stress levels.
generation.structural_mediator: The nitrided layer creates a hard, nitride-rich surface that inhibits dislocation motion, while the subsequent laser shock peening reduces microcracking and superficial roughness and introduces a compressive stress state that further mitigates crack initiation.
generation.mechanism: Low-temperature plasma nitriding infuses nitrogen to form hard TiN/Ti2N phases without excessive surface embrittlement. The following LSP process smooths residual surface irregularities and induces compressive stresses, which together improve wear resistance by preventing premature surface failure and crack propagation under cyclic loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the combined treatment is expected to raise the surface hardness by approximately 200–300% (relative to a baseline of ~421 HV) and reduce the wear rate by about 50% compared to nitriding alone. Fatigue life improvement under high-cycle conditions is also anticipated.
generation.baseline: Untreated Ti‑6Al‑4V alloy exhibits lower hardness, higher surface roughness, and greater wear rate under identical test conditions.
generation.boundary: The positive effects are anticipated for moderate nitriding parameters and optimized LSP conditions; excessive nitriding temperature or overly aggressive LSP may negate benefits. The improvement is also expected under standard lab tests but may require further validation for long-term service in harsh environments.
generation.uncertainty: While individual studies (e.g., PMC6384831 for plasma nitriding and PMC6073473 for LSP) report improved hardness and wear resistance, the combined sequential effect is untested. The degree to which LSP can effectively reduce the additional roughness induced by nitriding remains uncertain. This proposal extends findings from both approaches into a new hybrid process.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three groups of Ti‑6Al‑4V specimens: (1) untreated control; (2) low-temperature plasma nitriding only; and (3) combined treatment with plasma nitriding followed by laser shock peening. All specimens should have identical initial surface preparation. Subject specimens to standardized pin-on-disk wear tests and fatigue tests under controlled ambient conditions with the same load, sliding distance, and cycle parameters.
measurements: Wear rate (in mm³/Nm) from weight loss measurements
Fatigue life (number of cycles to failure) under cyclic loading
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the combined treatment group does not show a statistically significant improvement (for example, less than a 50% reduction in wear rate and less than a 20% increase in fatigue life) over the nitrided-only group, or if the surface roughness is not reduced relative to nitriding alone, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: LSP generated microdents on the surface of TC17 titanium alloy which induced plastic deformation and residual compressive stress on this material. The improvement in the impact-sliding wear resistance of TC17 titanium alloy after LSP was caused by the increased surface hardness and compressive residual stress. Under the same impact-sliding wear condition, the test sample treated by 7J pulse energy exhibited the best wear resistance, whereas the untreated sample showed the poorest results. As impact-sliding cycles increased, growth rates of wear area, wear depth, and wear volume of the three test samples varied. Therefore, lower growth rate was obtained when pulse energy was higher. The main wear mechanisms of the three test samples included delamination and abrasive wear.

By varying the microstructure and nitriding parameters, the fatigue strength of a material can be affected. Tokaji et al. [] reported that the fatigue strength of pure titanium was increased by nitriding, while it was decreased in the case of Ti-6Al-4V. Based on detailed observations of fatigue crack initiation, growth, and fracture surfaces, the improvement and the reduction in fatigue strength by nitriding of pure titanium and Ti-6Al-4V alloys were primarily attributed to enhanced crack initiation resistance and to premature crack initiation of the nitride layer, respectively. However, Farokhzadeh et al. [] achieved an improvement on the fatigue proprieties of the Ti-6Al-4V alloy plasma nitrided at a low temperature (600 °C). These results were different than those obtained by an elevated temperature treatment (900 °C) as well as conventional gas/plasma nitriding treatments reported in the literature [,,]. The thin morphology of the compound layer restricted the extent of premature crack initiation from the surface. Increased fatigue life of the plasma nitrided specimens in tests at higher stresses can be attributed to compressive residual stress in the nitride layers and in the nitrogen diffusion zone, thereby inhibiting crack nucleation at the alloy surface. This is in agreement with another study by Rodriguez et al. []. According to Farokhzadeh et al. [], the nitride layer reduces the extent of brittle failure on the specimen surface while the diffusion zone provides mechanical support. As per the study of Morita et al [], the formation of these layers after plasma nitriding increases the surface hardness of the alloy, which in turn increases the resistance to movement of dislocations and, as a consequence, increases the fatigue strength of the alloy. Rocha [], reported that delay in crack nucleation in plasma nitrided specimens is due to the difference in the Young modulus between the titanium alloy matrix (100 GPa) and the titanium nitrides formed on the plasma nitride surface (400 GPa). When high stresses are applied to the fragile nitride layer, it causes the nucleation and the growth of a crack in this layer.
